status: Fix pass on a branch: 23 commits fix 23 findings; 2 are partly fixed, 1 stays open, 1 is unchanged on purpose, and 5 are deferred. Fault tests T14, T19, T21, T26 and T27 were run again on development hosts and now pass. Atlas dependency tests D1 to D8 ran on the local site; they found one issue in Frappe itself (F33, kept out of the Atlas and Metal scores); F34 and F35 turned out not to be issues.

scenarios.scenario: `metald` crashes or is killed (`kill -9`).
scenarios.behavior: VMs run in their own `metal-vm@` systemd units and keep running. systemd restarts `metald`; it was ready again in 3 s. A guest writing every 0.2 s saw no pause above 0.4 s.
scenarios.ideal: Same as now.

scenarios.scenario: `metald` fails at startup 5 times in 10 s (bad config, pool not imported yet, wg0 not up).
scenarios.behavior: Confirmed in T29: 5 restarts in about 6 s, then systemd left the unit failed. After the cause was fixed, `metald` stayed down until `systemctl reset-failed` and a manual start. VMs kept running, unmanaged. `metald` also exits at start when WG Mesh setup fails (for example `wg0` not up yet at boot).
scenarios.ideal: Restart forever with a growing delay (`StartLimitIntervalSec=0`, `RestartSec=5`), and alert on a failed unit. See [F2].
scenarios.after_note: metald restarts every 5 s with no start limit (unit properties checked on two hosts).

scenarios.scenario: One VM or migration record on a host is corrupt.
scenarios.behavior: Startup validation fails for the whole daemon, so no VM on the host is managed.
scenarios.ideal: Quarantine only the bad record, start the daemon, and report the record in sync and the API. See [F3].
scenarios.after_note: Kept on purpose: skipping an unreadable record could reuse its user ID and addresses. metald now retries every 5 s until an operator fixes the file.

scenarios.scenario: A guest Firecracker process exits (kill or guest crash).
scenarios.behavior: The VM unit has `Restart=no`. The reconciler saw desired running, observed stopped, and started the VM 2 s later. ext4 journal recovery ran; all synced writes were present.
scenarios.ideal: Same, plus a crash-loop limit and a visible crash count on the VM.

scenarios.scenario: Atlas cannot reach one host (network cut or host API down).
scenarios.behavior: VMs on the host keep running. Power changes fail in 5 s with a clear error. Reading a VM takes 19 s and fails, so Desk forms hang. A create placed on the host in the first 2 min becomes a draft; after recovery the draft check gets 404 and deletes it. After 2 min without a capacity sample, placement skips the host. Sync writes one Error Log row every 10 s.
scenarios.ideal: Mark the host unreachable after the first failed sync, skip it in placement at once, fail VM reads fast with a cached last-known state, and log only state changes. See [F6].
scenarios.after_note: Failures are logged once an hour instead of on every pass. VM reads still wait for the Metal timeout.

scenarios.scenario: Atlas web, workers, and scheduler are down for hours.
scenarios.behavior: Hosts keep the last complete sync (peers, image policies, privileged addresses) and keep running every VM. No create, change, or migration is possible. Proxy routes and telemetry stop updating. Creates fail with an out-of-capacity error after 2 min ([F27]).
scenarios.ideal: Same, plus an external health check that pages when the scheduler stops.
scenarios.evidence: T3 (Atlas cut off from a host for 5 min) and T25 (scheduler stopped): running VMs were not affected.

scenarios.scenario: The host ZFS pool fills up (guests write more than the pool holds).
scenarios.behavior: Every guest on the host got I/O errors at once, even guests that did not write. Every reconcile failed because Metal could not write its state file. A stop request returned a bare HTTP 500. The host kept reporting 880 GiB free to placement. When space came back, Metal recovered by itself, but the guests stayed broken (SSH dead) until a restart, and each restart waited 30 s for a guest that could not shut down. A writer that waits for fsync got a clean EIO; all 93 acknowledged writes survived the event.
scenarios.ideal: Never overcommit physical space without a limit: count provisioned disk in placement, reserve space for Metal state, alert at 80 % pool use, and stop placement on the host. See [F1] and [F12].
scenarios.evidence: T4 and T4b on a development host.
scenarios.after_note: No overcommit: available storage is pool size less every provisioned disk. The state dataset keeps 1 GiB, and a full disk returns `507 host_storage_full`. Snapshots and image data can still fill a pool.

scenarios.scenario: An operator or an error aborts a disk-only migration after the destination VM booted, before Atlas commits.
scenarios.behavior: Confirmed in T21. The destination cold-booted and ran for 29 s before Atlas committed; the guest wrote and synced a file. An abort then deleted the destination disk and restarted the source from its pre-cutover disk. The file and 30 s of synced writes were lost, with no error or warning. Triggers: the Abort button while the status is `cutting_over`, `starting` or `finalizing` before commit, or a non-transient worker error during commit (the worker then fails the migration and aborts).
scenarios.ideal: Keep the destination paused or offline until finish, or allow only finish after the destination starts. See [F7].
scenarios.evidence: T21 on development hosts (Atlas worker frozen at cutover, abort sent while the destination ran).
scenarios.after_note: Retested T21: Metal refused rollback, Atlas finished the migration, the marker written on the destination survived.

scenarios.scenario: A VM uses an image that was archived more than 6 h ago, then restarts on a host that pruned the image.
scenarios.behavior: The VM cannot start: the kernel download fails.
scenarios.ideal: Keep image artifacts while any VM references the image. See [F8].
scenarios.after_note: Archived images keep their artifacts while any VM names them (unit tests).

scenarios.scenario: The Atlas queue Redis hangs (accepts connections but does not answer).
scenarios.behavior: Every code path that enqueues a job blocks for as long as Redis hangs. In the test an enqueue took the full 60 s pause. Web requests that enqueue (migrate, public IP changes) and scheduler ticks pile up.
scenarios.ideal: Set a socket timeout (for example 5 s) on the queue and cache Redis clients so a request fails fast with a retry-later error. Alert on Redis latency. See [F14].
scenarios.evidence: T5 on the local site (`CLIENT PAUSE 60000`).
scenarios.after_note: Retested D1: an enqueue blocked for the full 120 s and host sync stopped; all recovered at once. A socket timeout alone is not a fix, because of [F33].

scenarios.scenario: MariaDB for Atlas is down or full.
scenarios.behavior: Atlas web and jobs stop. Hosts keep running VMs with their last sync. When MariaDB returns, the scheduler and reconcilers continue from stored state; no host data depends on Atlas being up.
scenarios.ideal: Alert on database errors and free disk. Keep large log tables (Error Log, Metal Server Usage, Scheduled Job Log) under retention so a slow leak cannot fill the disk.
scenarios.evidence: Code reading. Not injected: no root access to the local database service.
scenarios.after_note: Tested D3, D3b, D4: with the database unreachable or read-only, web failed fast (no hang), host sync paused, a migration in copy finished, and all recovered within 10 s.

scenarios.scenario: `metald` on the destination is killed during the disk copy.
scenarios.behavior: The source stream broke. The destination restarted in 2 s, resumed the migration from its records, and completed. Data checksum and the guest counter were intact.
scenarios.ideal: Same as now.

scenarios.scenario: The network between source and destination drops all transfer packets for 2 min during the copy.
scenarios.behavior: The TCP stream stalled and resumed after the block (stall limit is 2 min). The migration completed in 172 s with a correct checksum. Atlas showed `copying` with no sign of the stall.
scenarios.ideal: Show stalled progress in Atlas (for example `no progress for 60 s`). See [F16].

scenarios.scenario: One node of a 3-node proxy cluster is down.
scenarios.behavior: Requests keep working: each node serves from its local route map with no quorum, and Route 53 drops the dead node after 2 failed checks 30 s apart. A client that cached the dead node's address can fail until the 120 s regional TTL ends, unless it tries the next address. Route writes (new site, domain change) return 503 while the node is down; Central retries them.
scenarios.ideal: Same. A majority write quorum ([F17]) would also keep route writes working, but that is a convenience, not a request failure.
scenarios.evidence: Code and handbook: `control-cluster` `_required_acknowledgements`, Route 53 health check (30 s interval, 2 failures), regional DNS TTL 120 s.

scenarios.scenario: The host root file system is 100 % full.
scenarios.behavior: VM restart and records kept working: VM state, chroots and disks live on ZFS. Only logs and package updates use the root file system. But Vector, the host log and metric shipper, failed with ENOSPC, hit its systemd start limit, and stayed dead after space came back. Host telemetry and logs stopped silently.
scenarios.ideal: Restart Vector without a start limit and alert when a host stops sending telemetry. Alert on root disk use. See [F28].
scenarios.after_note: Vector now restarts every 5 s with no start limit (checked on a host).

scenarios.scenario: A whole host reboots.
scenarios.behavior: The host was gone for 4 min 42 s. metald was ready 3 s after boot and all 6 VMs ran 5 s after boot. WireGuard peers and WG Mesh came back; cross-host mesh traffic worked.
scenarios.ideal: Same. Customers still see the full hardware restart time; a planned reboot should drain the host first.

scenarios.scenario: 20 creates arrive at the same moment on a 3-host region.
scenarios.behavior: 7 were placed across all hosts, 13 were rejected at once with `placement_busy`. No duplicates and no double booking.
scenarios.ideal: Same; clients retry `placement_busy`. This is the accepted fixed placement deadline.

scenarios.scenario: Object storage is unreachable while a host needs an image it has not cached.
scenarios.behavior: Metal retries the download forever with backoff and the VM starts within a minute after storage returns. For the whole outage the API shows state `unknown` with no error, because each retry clears the last error.
scenarios.ideal: Keep the last error visible until a pass succeeds, and report a clear phase such as `downloading image`. Cache every image that running VMs use. See [F20].
scenarios.after_note: The last VM error stays visible until the operation completes (unit test fails on the old code).

scenarios.scenario: Central is down for hours.
scenarios.behavior: Token checks keep the last valid key set. VM state webhooks retry 3 times (5 min, 30 min, 2 h), then stop for good.
scenarios.ideal: Periodic full state resync to Central, and ordering by `observed_at`. See [F19].
scenarios.after_note: Tested D6: failed state events are kept and retried, but a retried old event arrived after a newer one and left Central with the wrong state until the next change. See [F19].

scenarios.scenario: `wg0` is restarted on a host (`systemctl restart wg-quick@wg0`, a WireGuard package upgrade, or the Configure WireGuard action).
scenarios.behavior: Host WireGuard peers come back at the next Atlas sync (10 s), but the WG Mesh eBPF program on `wg0` is lost. Cross-host VM private traffic to and from that host stops and stays down. No error or metric shows it. A `metald` restart attaches the program again and traffic recovers at once. The 2026-10-16 incident fix covers only the Configure WireGuard script.
scenarios.ideal: `metald` checks the `wg0` hooks on every sync (or reacts to the interface coming back) and attaches them again. Alert when the hook is missing. See [F21].
scenarios.evidence: T14 on development hosts. Also seen earlier on a pre-production region.
scenarios.after_note: Retested T14: host sync attached the mesh hook again 18 s after the wg0 restart.

scenarios.scenario: The pool disk stops answering or fails (single vdev on software RAID 1).
scenarios.behavior: The pool uses `failmode=wait`, so all pool I/O blocks: guests freeze and `zfs` commands from Metal hang in the kernel where timeouts cannot stop them. Reconciler workers and API calls that touch ZFS can hang until the pool returns. ZFS sits on top of mdadm RAID 1, so ZFS can detect but not repair a bad block.
scenarios.ideal: Give ZFS the 2 disks as a mirror so it can repair bad blocks; alert on md and ZFS health (metrics exist); keep API health and sync paths free of ZFS calls that can block forever.
scenarios.evidence: Code reading and host layout. Not injected: no `zinject` on hosts.

scenarios.scenario: `metald` is killed while a new VM's image downloads.
scenarios.behavior: On restart Metal removed the unfinished import (no manifest), downloaded again, verified SHA-256, and started the VM 23 s after the kill.
scenarios.ideal: Same as now.

scenarios.scenario: The host of the IPv6 router VM fails, or the router service stops.
scenarios.behavior: Each IPv6 block has one router VM, and the provider routes the block to one host. All public IPv6 traffic for that block stops until the host or VM returns. Atlas keeps showing the router as `Active`; the handbook says Active does not prove forwarding works.
scenarios.ideal: Health-check forwarding through the router and alert. Document and automate the block move to a standby router on another host where the provider allows it. See [F23].
scenarios.evidence: Code reading and IPv6 router handbook.

scenarios.scenario: `metald` restarts while a VM sleeps (idle stop with saved memory).
scenarios.behavior: After the restart the traffic watch was armed again. A TCP connection woke the VM and it answered in 7 s with its memory restored.
scenarios.ideal: Same. The first packet can be lost while the VM wakes; clients retry.

scenarios.scenario: `metald` hangs (process alive, not answering), for example a deadlock or a ZFS call stuck in the kernel.
scenarios.behavior: systemd still shows the unit active and does not restart it: there is no watchdog. VMs keep running, but nothing is managed. In Atlas, a network change held the VM row lock for 17 s while Metal reads timed out, and another writer waited for the row the whole time.
scenarios.ideal: Add `WatchdogSec` and notify from the reconciler and API loops, so systemd restarts a hung daemon (VMs survive restarts, T1). Do not hold database row locks across Metal calls ([F5]). See [F24].
scenarios.after_note: Retested T19: the systemd watchdog restarted a frozen metald after 55 s; all VMs kept running.

scenarios.scenario: Many conflicting operations reach one VM at the same time (stop, start, restart, resize, metadata, keys).
scenarios.behavior: All requests returned in under 1 s (resize 4 s). Metal serialized them with its per-VM lock and generations, and converged in under 30 s with no stuck phase or error. The last stored power request wins.
scenarios.ideal: Same. Clients that need ordering must wait for the generation they caused.

scenarios.scenario: A host is lost for good (both disks fail, the provider reclaims the machine, or an operator wipes it).
scenarios.behavior: VM disks exist only on that host's ZFS pool. Atlas keeps the VM records, but there is no off-host copy to restore from. Data is lost unless the application inside the VM keeps its own backups.
scenarios.ideal: Scheduled, incremental ZFS snapshots sent off the host (to object storage or a peer host), with a restore-to-new-host action. Machine images already upload snapshots, so the transfer path exists. See [F25].
scenarios.evidence: Code reading: no backup or replica feature for VM disks.

scenarios.scenario: The Atlas database is lost or restored from an old backup.
scenarios.behavior: Hosts keep running every VM. Atlas forgets VMs created after the backup, and reuses their names; placement does not count them. Restoring needs the site backup together with `site_config.json` (encryption key). There is no tool to rebuild Atlas records from the hosts.
scenarios.ideal: Frequent Atlas database backups off the Atlas VM, a tested restore runbook, and a command that lists host VMs unknown to Atlas and imports or flags them. See [F9] and [F26].
scenarios.evidence: Code reading and host access handbook.
scenarios.after_note: Host sync now logs VMs that have no Atlas record. Importing them back is not built.

scenarios.scenario: Log tables grow without limit and fill the Atlas database disk.
scenarios.behavior: Error Log (14 days), Scheduled Job Log (7 days), Webhook Request Log (30 days) and capacity samples (3 h) have retention. SSH Task rows, which keep command output, have none. A flood of errors ([F6]) still fills Error Log within its 14 days.
scenarios.ideal: Retention for SSH Task and Metal Server Console Log, and an alert on database size.
scenarios.evidence: Local site: Log Settings and table sizes.
scenarios.after_note: Checked D7: the 14-day Error Log cleanup works. The sync-failure flood is fixed by [F6].

scenarios.scenario: `metald` on the destination is killed during cutover (after the source stopped).
scenarios.behavior: The daemon restarted, continued from its checkpoint, and the migration completed 4 s later with intact data.
scenarios.ideal: Same as now.

scenarios.scenario: `metald` on the source is killed while it stops the VM for cutover.
scenarios.behavior: The migration completed 6 s later. Data intact, and the source disk and records were removed.
scenarios.ideal: Same as now.

scenarios.scenario: An operator stops `metal.service` for maintenance, then starts it.
scenarios.behavior: All VMs kept running without a pause. On start, `metald` adopted every serial console from the systemd descriptor store.
scenarios.ideal: Same as now.

scenarios.scenario: A new `metald` build fails on a host during a rollout.
scenarios.behavior: `upgrade-metald.sh` checks the binary hash and version, waits up to 120 s for ready, checks that no VM stopped, and restores the previous build otherwise. The rollout stops at the first failed host (canary first).
scenarios.ideal: Same. A build with new state patches cannot roll back by design; ship those with extra care.
scenarios.evidence: Code reading of the upgrade script and Metald Update.

scenarios.scenario: The Atlas scheduler stops, or the default job queue falls more than 2 min behind.
scenarios.behavior: Host sync stops, every capacity sample becomes older than 2 min, and placement rejects every create with `No Metal Server has capacity. Retry later.` Existing VMs are not affected. Creates recover 10 s after sync resumes. Host syncs share the default queue with 15-min image transfers and provider calls, and an unreachable host holds a worker for up to 30 s, so a few bad hosts can starve sync for all hosts.
scenarios.ideal: Run host sync on its own queue and workers with a short timeout. Return a distinct `capacity_data_stale` error. Alert when the newest capacity sample is older than 1 min. See [F27].
scenarios.after_note: Placement fails fast with "Some Metal Servers have not reported their capacity" and orders no new host (D8). Creates work again within 20 s of the scheduler coming back. The usual way the scheduler stops is [F33], an issue in Frappe that is not scored here.

scenarios.scenario: The host NAT table is flushed (`iptables -t nat -F`, a firewall package reload, or an operator mistake).
scenarios.behavior: Metal re-added the per-VM public IPv4 SNAT and DNAT rules within 12 s. The shared masquerade rule for `10.0.0.0/8` is added only by the `metald` start script, so VMs without a public IPv4 had no IPv4 internet until `metald` restarts.
scenarios.ideal: Let the reconciler own the masquerade rule too and check it on every pass, like the per-VM rules. See [F29].
scenarios.after_note: Retested: a timer restored the masquerade rule within 30 s.

scenarios.scenario: The host filter table is flushed.
scenarios.behavior: Metal re-added the per-VM public IPv4 FORWARD rules. The rule that drops guest traffic to the host private network was not re-added. A direct test with that rule gone still could not reach another host's migration port, so another layer blocks it; one layer of defence stays missing until `metald` restarts.
scenarios.ideal: Reconcile the isolation rule on every pass, or move host rules into one nftables table that Metal owns and checks. Alert when it is missing. See [F30].
scenarios.after_note: Retested: a timer restored the private-network drop rule after 23 s.

scenarios.scenario: Atlas loses contact with the destination host at cutover for longer than 10 min (network partition, Atlas outage, destination API hang).
scenarios.behavior: The destination finished cutover by itself and ran the guest for 11 min. Atlas hit its 10-min visibility timeout, marked the migration `canceling`, and sent abort when the network returned. Metal deleted the destination disk and restarted the source from its old disk. 11 min of synced guest writes were lost, with no operator action. The migration ended `failed` with `destination_unreachable`.
scenarios.ideal: After the destination started the guest, never roll back automatically: keep retrying finish (the destination already holds the newest disk). Abort only before the source stops. See [F7].
scenarios.after_note: Same path as the T21 retest: at `ready` the destination refuses rollback, so Atlas finishes once contact returns.

scenarios.scenario: Customers create VMs with large disks.
scenarios.behavior: Placement put 8 VMs of 512 GiB each (4 TiB) on one host with an 864 GiB pool, because it reads physical free space and new thin disks use almost none. Nothing limits overcommit, so the host pool fills as guests write ([S7]).
scenarios.ideal: Count provisioned disk against an explicit overcommit ratio per host, and stop placement at a pool-use threshold. See [F12].
scenarios.evidence: T31 on the local site and development hosts.
scenarios.after_note: Checked on a host: 53,248 MiB of provisioned disks now lower available storage from 837,557 MiB to 804,096 MiB.

scenarios.scenario: The destination host dies for good after the source stopped the VM for cutover.
scenarios.behavior: The source VM stays stopped and locked: Metal never expires a stopped source. Atlas keeps the migration `canceling` and keeps the VM action lock, so the customer VM stays down and no other action (start, migrate, resize) is allowed. There is no force-rollback action in Atlas.
scenarios.ideal: An operator action (Dangerous Actions) that rolls the source back without the destination after confirming the destination is gone, and an alert for migrations stuck in `canceling`. See [F32].
scenarios.evidence: Code reading, following T28 (Atlas waits in `canceling` while the destination is unreachable).
scenarios.after_note: An operator runs Dangerous Actions > Restore Source once the destination has not reported for 15 minutes. Metal starts and unlocks the source; a destination that returns is discarded. Tested end to end on development hosts. Writes on the lost destination after cutover are gone.

scenarios.scenario: The cache Redis hangs, or answers with errors.
scenarios.behavior: A hang freezes every web request and stops host sync until Redis answers. With a socket timeout, requests fail fast, but the timeout error kills the scheduler thread of the Frappe runner for good.
scenarios.ideal: Requests fail fast and the scheduler survives a Redis error: catch errors per scheduler tick, and restart a dead scheduler thread. Alert on the scheduler heartbeat.
scenarios.evidence: D2 and D2b on the local site.

findings.problem: VM volumes are thin ZFS clones with no reservation. The Metal state dataset has no reservation either. The pool is shared.
findings.effect: A full pool breaks every guest on the host at the same time (I/O errors, then dead services until restart). Metal cannot write records, so every reconcile fails and an API stop returns HTTP 500.
findings.fix: Reserve space for `metal/state`. Alert and stop placement at a pool-use threshold. Count provisioned disk in placement ([F12]).
findings.resolution: Fixed: metald counts provisioned disks, and the state dataset keeps a 1 GiB reservation.

findings.problem: Hosts report pool free space from `zpool list` as available storage. Thin VM disks use little space at first, so placement can sell the same space many times.
findings.effect: No limit on disk overcommit. Together with [F1] this leads to a full pool as guests grow. During T4 the host reported 880 GiB free while every dataset had 0 bytes available.
findings.fix: Report storage as pool size minus provisioned volume sizes (or apply an explicit overcommit ratio), and read `available` from `zfs get`, not `zpool list`.
findings.verified: T4 and T31: 4 TiB of disks placed on an 864 GiB pool
findings.resolution: Fixed: available storage is the smaller of free pool space and pool size less every provisioned disk. Verified on a host.

findings.problem: `metal.service` uses the default start limit (5 starts in 10 s) with `RestartSec=1`.
findings.effect: A transient startup failure (for example WG Mesh setup before `wg0` is ready at boot) leaves the daemon failed for good. Nothing on the host manages VMs until an operator runs `systemctl reset-failed metal`.
findings.fix: Set `StartLimitIntervalSec=0` and a longer `RestartSec`, and alert on a failed unit.
findings.resolution: Fixed: `StartLimitIntervalSec=0`, `RestartSec=5`.

findings.problem: One unreadable VM or migration record stops daemon startup.
findings.effect: Blast radius is the whole host instead of one VM.
findings.fix: Quarantine the bad record and start the daemon for the other VMs.
findings.resolution: Not changed on purpose: skipping a bad record could hand its user ID and addresses to a new VM. With F2 fixed, metald retries every 5 s until an operator fixes the file.

findings.problem: The VM reconciler runs 4 workers and waits for the whole pass. One VM operation can take up to 35 min (for example an image download).
findings.effect: 4 slow VMs delay stop, restart, and delete for every other VM on the host.
findings.fix: Track in-flight VMs and start work for idle VMs without waiting for the slowest one.
findings.resolution: Fixed: VM operations share slots across passes; a pass does not wait for slow VMs.

findings.problem: Network and route changes lock the Virtual Machine row (`FOR UPDATE`) and then call Metal twice.
findings.effect: A slow host holds the row lock for up to about 90 s, so other writers hit lock wait timeouts.
findings.fix: Do not hold a row lock across a Metal call. Compare Metal generations instead.
findings.verified: T19: a second writer waited 17 s for the row while Metal hung
findings.resolution: Fixed: a per-VM file lock serializes network changes; no row lock waits on Metal.

findings.problem: Each failed host sync, draft check, and termination check writes an Error Log row on every pass.
findings.effect: One unreachable host writes about 8,640 rows a day for sync alone, plus rows per VM.
findings.fix: Log the first failure and state changes. Keep the last error and a failure count on the Metal Server.
findings.verified: T3: 30 rows in 5 min for one host
findings.resolution: Fixed: repeated sync and reconcile failures are logged once an hour.

findings.problem: A disk-only migration cold-boots the guest on the destination before Atlas commits ownership. Abort is still allowed in that window, and Atlas aborts by itself when the destination is silent for 10 min. Abort deletes the destination disk and restores the source from the pre-cutover snapshot.
findings.effect: Writes that the guest made and synced on the destination are lost after an abort, silently. The guest goes back in time by the length of the window.
findings.fix: Once the destination has started the guest, allow only finish: reject abort in Atlas and Metal, and make the worker retry commit instead of failing. Or keep the destination guest paused (and with no network) until Atlas commits, so it cannot write.
findings.verified: T21 (operator abort) and T28 (11-min Atlas-to-destination network cut, no operator): synced guest writes lost
findings.resolution: Fixed: a disk-only destination refuses abort at `ready`, and Atlas finishes the migration instead. Retested T21.

findings.problem: Archived images lose their artifacts after the retention time even while VMs use them. Image cleanup counts a VM as a user of its image only while its reported state is running, stopped or paused, so a VM that is failing to start does not protect its image.
findings.effect: A VM with an archived image cannot start again after a restart, resize, or migration.
findings.fix: Keep the kernel and root file system artifacts while any VM references the image.
findings.where: Image reclaim in Atlas, `ensureImage` in Metal
findings.verified: Known open issue, seen on a pre-production host
findings.resolution: Fixed: artifacts are deleted only with the image record, after the last VM record.

findings.problem: No check compares the VMs on each host with Atlas records.
findings.effect: After an Atlas database restore, VMs created after the backup run on hosts without Atlas records. Placement does not count them.
findings.fix: Report unknown VM IDs from sync and show them on the Metal Server.
findings.resolution: Fixed: host sync logs VMs that have no Atlas record.

findings.problem: A disk resize stores `disk_mib` in Atlas in a later write after Metal accepts it.
findings.effect: If the Atlas write fails, placement counts the old, smaller disk.
findings.fix: Write the reservation before the Metal call, or read it from Metal state.
findings.resolution: Fixed: a retried resize repairs the stored disk size.

findings.problem: Terminal destination records stay on the host with no cleanup.
findings.effect: Directories collect over time. Seen 8 days after an aborted migration.
findings.fix: Remove terminal records after a retention time.
findings.resolution: Fixed: clean aborted destination records are removed after 7 days.

findings.problem: When Metal cannot write its state, API mutations return a bare `internal server error`.
findings.effect: Atlas shows `Metal request failed: internal server error`. The operator cannot see that the host disk is full.
findings.fix: Map `ENOSPC` to a stable error code such as `host_storage_full` with a clear message.
findings.resolution: Fixed: `ENOSPC` returns `507 host_storage_full`.

findings.problem: The Redis clients for the queue have no socket timeout.
findings.effect: A hung Redis blocks web requests and scheduler ticks with no limit. Workers are used up and the whole Atlas site stops answering.
findings.fix: Set `socket_timeout` and `socket_connect_timeout` on the Redis connections, and map the timeout to a retry-later error.
findings.where: Frappe Redis connection setup used by `frappe.enqueue`
findings.resolution: Open: owned by the bench Redis configuration (Pilot and Frappe). Not changed in Atlas.

findings.problem: Migration transfer rows store `0` throughput even for a 3.7 GiB transfer.
findings.effect: Operators cannot see the copy speed, which makes slow or stalled copies hard to find.
findings.fix: Store the measured throughput from Metal, or compute it from bytes and duration.
findings.resolution: Fixed: Atlas measures throughput from copied MiB and elapsed time.

findings.problem: A stalled copy shows the same `copying` status as a healthy one.
findings.effect: During the 2-min stall nothing in Atlas showed a problem.
findings.fix: Show the time since the last byte moved and warn after 60 s.
findings.resolution: Fixed: the migration status shows live bytes for the interval in flight.

findings.problem: Proxy and gateway clusters with 3 or fewer nodes require an acknowledgement from every node for each route write.
findings.effect: One node down blocks route writes in the region (new sites, domains) until it returns. Requests are not affected, and Central retries the writes.
findings.fix: Use a majority for writes and rely on snapshot catch-up for the stale node, or require at least 4 nodes in production.
findings.resolution: Deferred: route writes are retried by Central; requests keep working.

findings.problem: Machine image transfer marks the image `Failed` on any Metal client error, including timeouts and 502/503. The pending-transfer job skips Failed images.
findings.effect: A short host or network problem during an image upload fails the image for good. The staged snapshot on the host is pruned after 48 h.
findings.fix: Keep the status and retry when the error is retryable; fail only on a definite error.
findings.resolution: Fixed: a retryable Metal error keeps the transfer running and shows the error.

findings.problem: VM state reaches Central only through Frappe webhooks with 3 retries (5 min, 30 min, 2 h). Retries can deliver an older state after a newer one.
findings.effect: A Central outage longer than about 2.5 h loses state events for good. A late retry can make Central show a stale state.
findings.fix: Have Central drop events older than its stored `observed_at`, and add a periodic full state resync between Atlas and Central.
findings.resolution: Deferred: owned by Central.

findings.problem: Every reconcile phase sets the observed error to empty before it runs. A VM whose start fails on each pass shows no error between passes.
findings.effect: During a 5-min image download outage the API showed only `unknown` with no reason. Operators and customers cannot see why a VM does not start.
findings.fix: Clear the stored error only after a phase succeeds, and keep a failure count and the time of the last failure.
findings.resolution: Fixed: the stored error stays until the operation completes.

findings.problem: WG Mesh attaches its eBPF program to `wg0` only when `metald` starts. The fix for the 2026-10-16 incident makes `configure-wireguard.sh` restart `metald`, but any other `wg0` restart (manual `systemctl restart wg-quick@wg0`, a package upgrade hook, a unit dependency restart) still removes the program for good.
findings.effect: Any `wg0` restart cuts the private network of every VM on the host until someone restarts `metald`. Nothing reports it.
findings.fix: Make the mesh hook check part of each sync: if the program is missing, attach it again (the attach is already safe to repeat). Export a metric for hook presence.
findings.verified: T14 fault injection (repeats the root cause of the 2026-10-16 incident through another path)
findings.resolution: Fixed: each host sync checks the mesh hooks and configures the mesh again when one is missing. Retested T14.

findings.problem: The ZFS pool is created on a single md RAID 1 device instead of a ZFS mirror of the 2 disks.
findings.effect: ZFS detects checksum errors but cannot repair them, and md RAID 1 cannot tell which copy is good. Silent corruption on one disk can reach guests.
findings.fix: Create the pool as a ZFS mirror of the 2 partitions for new hosts. Plan a migration path for existing hosts (drain, rebuild).
findings.resolution: Deferred: needs host rebuilds.

findings.problem: Each public IPv6 block depends on one router VM on one host, with no health check of forwarding.
findings.effect: One host failure stops public IPv6 for every VM that uses the block, and Atlas still shows the router as Active.
findings.fix: Add a forwarding health check that marks the router unhealthy and alerts. Keep a runbook (or automation) to move the block to a standby router.
findings.resolution: Deferred: needs a standby router design.

findings.problem: `metal.service` has no systemd watchdog.
findings.effect: A hung daemon stays hung: no restart, no alert from systemd. All VM management on the host stops until someone notices.
findings.fix: Set `WatchdogSec=` and send `WATCHDOG=1` from a loop that proves the reconciler and API still make progress.
findings.resolution: Fixed: metald pings the systemd watchdog; `WatchdogSec=60`. Retested T19.

findings.problem: There is no off-host copy of VM disks: no scheduled snapshot shipping, no replica, no restore-to-new-host flow.
findings.effect: Losing one host's pool loses the data of every VM on it. RAID 1 protects only against one disk failure, not against host loss, provider reclaim, operator error, or pool corruption.
findings.fix: Add scheduled incremental snapshot shipping (the machine image upload path already streams ZFS data to object storage) with a retention policy and a restore action. Make it at least opt-in per VM, and on by default for tenant data VMs.
findings.where: Metal storage and Atlas VM module
findings.resolution: Deferred: needs off-host storage and an architecture.

findings.problem: Atlas cannot rebuild its VM records from the hosts.
findings.effect: After an Atlas database loss or old restore, operators cannot find or adopt VMs that exist only on hosts.
findings.fix: Add a reconcile command that compares `GET /v1/vms` on every host with Atlas records and reports or imports the differences.
findings.resolution: Partial: unknown VMs are now reported (F9). Import is not built.

findings.problem: Placement uses only capacity samples newer than 2 min, and those samples depend on the scheduler plus the shared default queue.
findings.effect: Any scheduler stop or queue backlog over 2 min turns into a region-wide create outage with a misleading out-of-capacity error. Nothing alerts on stale samples.
findings.fix: Give host sync a dedicated queue and worker pool with a short job timeout; return a separate stale-data error; alert on sample age and on a disabled scheduler.
findings.resolution: Partial: stale samples no longer order a new host and the error says why. A separate queue does not help, because one worker group serves all queues.

findings.problem: Vector on hosts uses the default systemd start limit. One transient failure (for example a full disk) leaves it dead for good.
findings.effect: Host logs and metrics, including the metald push to Datum, stop with no alert. Operators lose visibility exactly when a host has problems.
findings.fix: Set `StartLimitIntervalSec=0` and `Restart=always` with a delay for Vector, and alert in Atlas or Insights when a host has sent no telemetry for 5 min.
findings.verified: Seen after T11 on a development host
findings.resolution: Fixed: Vector drop-in with no start limit and `RestartSec=5`.

findings.problem: The shared IPv4 masquerade rule is created only by `ExecStartPre=network-setup` when `metald` starts.
findings.effect: Any flush of the NAT table cuts IPv4 internet for every VM on the host without a public IPv4, and nothing repairs it until `metald` restarts.
findings.fix: Ensure the masquerade rule in the network reconcile path (it already re-creates per-VM rules) and export a metric when it is missing.
findings.resolution: Fixed: a 30-second timer runs the host network setup again.

findings.problem: The FORWARD rule that drops guest traffic to the host private network is created only by the `metald` start script.
findings.effect: After a filter table flush, one isolation layer between guests and the host private network stays missing until `metald` restarts. In the test another layer still blocked the traffic.
findings.fix: Own the rule in the network reconciler next to the per-VM rules, and check it on every pass.
findings.verified: T27 fault injection and a direct connection test
findings.resolution: Fixed: the same timer restores the drop rule.

findings.problem: Each host sync (every 10 s) saves the `Virtual Machine State` document of every VM on the host, with a commit each, even when nothing changed.
findings.effect: Measured 3.5 ms per VM on the local site. At 100 hosts with 200 VMs each that is about 70 s of database work every 10 s. Sync then falls behind, and stale capacity blocks every create ([F27]).
findings.fix: Write a state row only when its status changes, keep `synced_at` once per host, and batch the writes in one transaction.
findings.resolution: Fixed: only new or changed VM states are saved as documents; unchanged ones get one update per host.

findings.problem: Source rollback is driven only by the destination. If the destination host is lost after the source stopped, nothing can restart the source, and Atlas has no force action.
findings.effect: A hardware failure of the destination during cutover keeps the customer VM down until the destination returns or someone edits host records by hand.
findings.fix: Add a Metal source API and an Atlas Dangerous Action to roll back a stopped source when the destination is confirmed gone, plus an alert on migrations in `canceling` for more than 15 min.
findings.resolution: Fixed as a manual Dangerous Action: Restore Source, allowed only before commit and after 15 minutes without a destination report. A returning destination is discarded. Tested end to end.

findings.problem: The scheduler loop of Frappe (`start_scheduler`) has no error handling. A Redis error in it ends the scheduler thread. The lite-mode runner never starts it again; the worker-pool starts it again only at the RQ maintenance interval (about 10 minutes). The process stays alive, so systemd does not restart it.
findings.effect: Host sync stops, every capacity sample goes stale, and placement rejects every create until the scheduler comes back (7+ minutes in the test, until a manual reload).
findings.fix: In Frappe: catch and log errors per scheduler tick and keep looping; have the runner watch its scheduler thread. In Atlas: alert on the scheduler heartbeat and `atlas_host_sync_age_seconds`.
findings.resolution: Open: tracked for a fix in frappe/frappe. Not counted in the Atlas and Metal scores.

findings.problem: The migration worker treats a lost database connection as a definite error and tries to fail the migration.
findings.effect: During a long outage the fail write also fails, so nothing changes (D3b). A blip that ends between the two writes can fail a healthy migration.
findings.fix: Treat lost-connection errors (2003, 2006, 2013, interface errors) as transient.
findings.verified: D3b fault injection and code reading
findings.resolution: Not reachable: Frappe does not reconnect inside a job, so after a lost connection the worker's `frappe.db.rollback()` raises (`2006`) before it can fail the migration. The next reconcile resumes it (D3b). Checked by killing a live connection. No change.

findings.problem: The VM state webhook sends `observed_at` in local site time with no time zone.
findings.effect: Central cannot order events safely when its time zone differs from the Atlas site.
findings.fix: Add an optional field with a time zone (for example Unix seconds) and have Central order by it.
findings.resolution: Not an issue: Atlas sites run in UTC, and Central reads `observed_at` as UTC.

items.text: Draft is committed before the Metal call; the VM name is the Metal ID, so a retry is idempotent (T3).
A draft whose create never reached Metal is deleted after a confirmed 404 (T3).
Concurrent creates do not double-book a host (T9).
Placement can pick a host that stopped answering less than 2 min ago (T3).
Placement does not count provisioned thin disk, so disk can be oversold without limit ([F12]).
While an image downloads, Atlas shows state `unknown` instead of a clear starting phase (T12).
Destroy runs in checkpointed steps (runtime, network, storage) and resumes after a crash.
Atlas deletes the record only after Metal confirms absence; all host resources were removed (T9).
A host that cannot write state (full pool) cannot destroy a VM to free space ([F1]).
Metal stores desired state and the reconciler converges; a killed guest restarts in 2 s (T2).
A guest that cannot shut down costs the full 30 s graceful timeout per restart (T4).
No crash-loop limit or crash counter for a guest that keeps failing.
Destination daemon crash during copy: resumed and completed with intact data (T6).
2-min network cut during copy: stream resumed, data intact (T7).
Atlas commits ownership before Metal destroys the source; finish and abort are exclusive.
A 10-min Atlas-to-destination network cut at cutover makes Atlas roll back and lose the guest's writes (T28).
Abort after the destination booted discards destination writes ([F7]).
Stall and throughput are not visible in Atlas ([F15], [F16]).
No operator action to recover a source when the destination host is lost ([F32]).
Hosts keep running VMs and last sync when Atlas is down or cut off (T3).
Controller sets (peers, images, privileged addresses) are complete and replace the old set, so a missed sync heals on the next one.
A host that cannot reach Atlas is not marked unreachable; errors go to Error Log every 10 s ([F6]).
Crash and reboot recovery: ready in 3 s, VMs restarted after boot (T1, T8).
State files are written atomically with fsync.
Start limit can leave the daemon failed after 5 quick failures ([F2]).
One corrupt record stops the whole daemon ([F3]).
fsync-acknowledged guest writes survive a full pool (T4b).
No reservation for Metal state, no pool alert, no placement stop near full ([F1]).
Downloads verify SHA-256 and retry transient errors; partial imports are removed.
Archived images lose artifacts while VMs still use them ([F8]).
A transient Metal error during image upload marks the image Failed for good ([F18]).
Central outage: the last valid key set stays in use for token checks.
Queue Redis hang blocks requests with no timeout ([F14]).
VM state webhooks to Central stop after 3 retries (about 2.5 h) and can arrive out of order ([F19]).
Each node serves from its local route map; DNS health checks drop a bad node.
With 3 or fewer nodes, one bad node blocks route writes ([F17]).
metald rollouts use a canary batch, health checks, and stop on the first failure.
Daemon upgrade restarts in place; VMs keep running.
Provider create is idempotent by name; setup runs as one deduplicated job and each step is safe to repeat.
Storage setup refuses a device that has any partition table, file system or signature, so it cannot wipe data.
The state dataset gets no space reservation ([F1]); the pool is one md device, not a ZFS mirror ([F22]).
WireGuard peers are re-applied on every sync, so a `wg0` restart heals peers in 10 s (T14).
The WG Mesh program is not re-attached after a `wg0` restart ([F21]).
Per-VM NAT and FORWARD rules are reconciled; the shared masquerade and isolation rules are not ([F29], [F30]).
